tagline: Along the mountain rim to a town that studies the Sun.
intro: Two miles south of Cloudcroft, named for the clouds that hug its hillsides, NM 6563 leaves NM 130 and runs about 15 miles south along the front rim of the Sacramento Mountains, through pine, aspen and fir, with lookouts onto the basin some 5,000 feet below. Partway along is Dirty Drawers Canyon, named, the local story goes, for a woman whose hygiene was in question, like her reputation.

The highway number is the wavelength in angstroms of the hydrogen-alpha line, which the observatory at the end of the road uses to find flares on the Sun. Only two other state highways in New Mexico carry four digits.

moments.title: Haynes Canyon Vista
moments.text: From the overlook the landmarks run out across the basin to the Oscura and San Andres peaks and the white of White Sands.

moments.title: The planets
moments.text: In 2011 the observatory put up signs along the highway naming the planets, spaced as a model of the solar system at one to 250 million.

moments.title: Sunspot
moments.text: The observatory community at the end of the road took its name in a vote that the observatory director, John Evans, is said to have rigged.

sources.label: New Mexico True, Sunspot Scenic Byway
